The Amsterdam Exchange was the building and market where merchants and brokers met every working day to trade goods, bills of exchange and shares. It was first built in 1608 to 1611, and it is often called the world's first stock exchange, because shares of the Dutch East India Company were traded there from the start.

Merchants had met in the open air on a bridge before the city gave them a hall, modelled on London's Royal Exchange and the earlier bourse of Antwerp. Trading took place at fixed hours, and each trade had its own spot around the courtyard.

What was traded:

  • Grain, spices, timber and hundreds of other goods, often by sample or for future delivery.
  • Bills of exchange, which linked Amsterdam's money market to the rest of Europe.
  • VOC shares, and contracts on them: futures, options and short sales were all in use in the 1600s.

Fernand Braudel calls an exchange a fair that never closes, and this one was the engine of Amsterdam's age at the centre. A Jewish merchant, Joseph de la Vega, described its tricks in 1688 in Confusion of Confusions, the first book about a stock market.

The original building was pulled down in the 1830s and replaced several times. The exchange carried on, and in 2000 it merged with the exchanges of Brussels and Paris to form Euronext.
